title: Eating disorders and MEED
blurb: Use NICE NG69 and the MEED risk tool to match treatment to the eating disorder, spot red flags and refeed safely.
question: Amira, 22, has anorexia nervosa. At clinic her heart rate is 38 bpm, she has lost 1.2 kg in each of the last 2 weeks and she cannot rise from a squat without using her hands. Her BMI is 14.2. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: Eating disorders kill through the body
teach.body: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder and OSFED are mental disorders, but the immediate danger is usually physical: bradycardia, electrolyte loss from purging, hypothermia, muscle weakness and refeeding syndrome. NICE NG69 sets the treatments; the Royal College of Psychiatrists' MEED guidance (2022, which replaced MARSIPAN and Junior MARSIPAN) sets the physical risk ratings. In plain English: treat the mind, but watch the body like a medical patient.
teach.cite: NICE NG69 (2017, updated 2020); RCPsych CR233 MEED (2022)

head: Disorder
Adults
Children and young people
rows: BED-focused guided self-help, then group CBT-ED
teach.caption: Guided self-help that is unacceptable or ineffective after 4 weeks steps up to CBT-ED (NG69 1.4.4, 1.5.4). No medication as the sole treatment for binge eating disorder.

Also red: systolic BP under 90, adult QTc over 450 ms (women) or over 430 ms (men), potassium under 2.5 mmol/L, acute food refusal. For a red finding the tool says refer to A&E and consult a medical specialist.

teach.h: From red flag to safe refeeding

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: Obs, BMI trend, SUSS, ECG, bloods

teach.caption: NG69 1.11.10: use a standard operating procedure for refeeding that refers to MEED.

teach.body: When a starved body is fed, insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Blood levels can fall sharply in the first days of refeeding, with risk of arrhythmia, heart failure, confusion and seizures. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark. NG69 asks for staff trained to recognise it and a refeeding protocol that avoids both refeeding syndrome and under-nutrition. Plain English: start feeding, but check the bloods closely, because too little food is also dangerous.

items.label: SUSS score: cannot rise without hands

teach.caption: SUSS = Sit Up, Squat, Stand test of muscle power.

teach.h: NG69 points nurses are tested on
items: Do not use single measures such as BMI or duration of illness to decide whether to offer treatment (NG69 1.2.8).
Do not use an absolute weight or BMI threshold to decide on admission; weigh the rate of loss and physical risk (1.11.2-1.11.3).
Do not discharge solely because a healthy weight is reached (1.11.4).
Vomiting: avoid brushing teeth straight after, rinse with non-acid mouthwash, regular dental reviews (1.10.6).
Laxatives and diuretics do not reduce calorie absorption; reduce gradually (1.10.7).

teach.h: She refuses treatment and her life is at risk

children.label: Mental Health Act 1983
children.sub: Feeding is treatment for the disorder

teach.caption: NG69 1.12.1-1.12.3.

teach.body: Amira's heart rate under 40, weight loss of 1 kg or more a week and a SUSS score of 0 to 1 are all MEED red flags, even though her BMI of 14.2 sits in the amber band. The nurse does not wait for her BMI to fall below 13. She escalates the same day for urgent medical review and admission for medical stabilisation, arranges an ECG and bloods including phosphate and potassium, and explains to Amira why her body needs protecting now.

teach.text: BMI is not the gatekeeper. A person with a 'not so low' BMI can be at high risk from rapid weight loss, bradycardia, hypothermia or purging-related low potassium. NG69 says no single measure decides treatment, and MEED rates each parameter separately. And remember MEED replaced MARSIPAN in 2022.

items: Adult anorexia: CBT-ED, MANTRA or SSCM. Young people: FT-AN. Bulimia and BED: guided self-help first.
MEED red (adults): BMI under 13, HR under 40, temp under 35.5 C, loss 1 kg or more a week, SUSS 0 to 1, K+ under 2.5.
Refeeding syndrome: phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall in the first days; follow a refeeding protocol.
Compulsory treatment under the MHA if life is at risk and treatment is refused.

summary: You can now choose the NG69 first-line treatment for each eating disorder and rate physical risk with the MEED parameters. You can also explain refeeding syndrome, why BMI alone never decides care, and when the Mental Health Act applies.

A.q: Which psychological treatment does NICE NG69 recommend first for a 15-year-old with anorexia nervosa?
options: Individual CBT-ED delivered over 40 sessions
Anorexia-focused family therapy (FT-AN)
Specialist supportive clinical management
A bulimia-focused guided self-help programme
A.why: For children and young people with anorexia nervosa, NG69 recommends anorexia-focused family therapy (FT-AN) first.

whyNot.0: Individual CBT-ED is an adult option and a second-line option for young people when FT-AN is unsuitable.
whyNot.2: SSCM is one of the three adult options, not the first choice for a young person.
whyNot.3: Guided self-help is for bulimia nervosa in adults, not anorexia.

A.q: Using the MEED tool, which adult finding is rated red (high impending risk to life)?
options: Resting heart rate of 46 bpm
Body mass index of 14.5
Tympanic temperature of 35.2 C
Weight loss of 0.7 kg a week
A.why: MEED rates a temperature under 35.5 C as red in adults.

whyNot.0: A heart rate of 40 to 50 is amber; red is under 40.
whyNot.1: A BMI of 13 to 14.9 is amber in adults; red is under 13.
whyNot.3: Loss of 0.5 to 1 kg a week is amber; red is 1 kg or more a week.

A.q: Which blood result is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
options: Low serum phosphate
High serum sodium
Raised serum calcium
High serum potassium
A.why: Refeeding drives phosphate (with potassium and magnesium) into cells, so hypophosphataemia in the first days of refeeding is the hallmark.

whyNot.1: Sodium is not the defining electrolyte; fluid shifts more often cause oedema.
whyNot.2: Calcium is not raised in refeeding syndrome.
whyNot.3: Potassium falls, not rises, as it moves into cells.

B.q: Leon, 30, has bulimia nervosa and asks for help. Which treatment should be considered first under NICE NG69?
options: Bulimia-focused guided self-help
Fluoxetine as a first treatment on its own
Admission for supervised meals
Group CBT-ED for 16 weeks
B.why: NG69 recommends considering bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help for adults first, stepping up to individual CBT-ED if it is unacceptable or ineffective after 4 weeks.

whyNot.1: Medication alone is not the NG69 first step for bulimia nervosa.
whyNot.2: Admission is for severe physical or psychiatric risk, not first-line treatment.
whyNot.3: Group CBT-ED is the step-up option for binge eating disorder, not bulimia.

B.q: A ward nurse notices that Priya, who has bulimia nervosa, brushes her teeth immediately after each episode of vomiting. What advice fits NICE NG69?
options: Brush straight away with a high-fluoride toothpaste
Rinse with an acidic mouthwash to strip off residue
Rinse with a non-acid mouthwash; avoid brushing at once
Chew acidic fruit afterwards to clear the mouth
B.why: NG69 1.10.6 advises avoiding brushing teeth immediately after vomiting, rinsing with non-acid mouthwash and avoiding highly acidic food and drink, plus regular dental reviews.

whyNot.0: Brushing straight after vomiting scrubs acid into softened enamel.
whyNot.1: An acidic rinse adds to enamel erosion.
whyNot.3: Highly acidic foods should be avoided.

B.q: A colleague says a young woman with anorexia nervosa does not need admission because her BMI is 15. Her weight has dropped 1.5 kg a week for 3 weeks and her pulse is 38 bpm. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as admission starts below BMI 13
Agree, and recheck her weight in a month
Admission depends on BMI and duration alone
Rate of loss and pulse put her at high risk
B.why: NG69 1.11.2-1.11.3: no absolute BMI threshold decides admission; rate of weight loss (over 1 kg a week) and parameters such as bradycardia under 40 are MEED red flags.

whyNot.0: There is no BMI threshold for admission in NG69.
whyNot.1: Red flags need same-day medical review, not a month's wait.
whyNot.2: NG69 says not to use single measures such as BMI or duration to decide treatment.

C.q: On day 3 of refeeding on a medical ward, Hannah, 19, with anorexia nervosa, becomes confused and her ECG shows new ectopic beats. Her phosphate was normal on admission. What is the most likely cause and first action?
options: Starvation ketosis; increase her calories now
Refeeding syndrome; urgent bloods and medical review
Anxiety about weight gain; offer reassurance and distraction
Dehydration; give a litre of oral fluid over the next hour
C.why: New confusion and arrhythmia in the first days of refeeding suggest refeeding syndrome (falling phosphate, potassium, magnesium); urgent bloods and medical review, following the refeeding protocol.

whyNot.0: Pushing calories faster could worsen refeeding syndrome.
whyNot.2: Physical signs need medical assessment before any psychological explanation.
whyNot.3: Arrhythmia and confusion on day 3 point to electrolyte shift, not simple dehydration.

C.q: Ruth, 34, has severe anorexia nervosa. Her potassium is 2.3 mmol/L, she refuses admission and says she is fine. The team believes she needs inpatient refeeding to survive. Which framework does NICE NG69 point to?
options: The Mental Capacity Act best-interests process alone
Waiting until she agrees to a voluntary admission
The Mental Health Act 1983 compulsory framework
A deprivation of liberty authorisation at home
C.why: NG69 1.12.1: if physical health is at serious risk, the person does not consent and can only be treated safely as an inpatient, follow the Mental Health Act 1983; feeding is treatment of the disorder.

whyNot.0: Where a person objects to admission for a mental disorder, the MHA is the framework NG69 names.
whyNot.1: A potassium under 2.5 is a MEED red flag; waiting risks her life.
whyNot.3: DoLS applies in hospitals and care homes, not her own home, and cannot authorise treatment for mental disorder she objects to; NG69 1.12.1 names the MHA.

C.q: Tom, 26, has binge eating disorder. He asks for a weight-loss diet alongside group CBT-ED. What should the nurse advise?
options: Start a calorie-controlled diet alongside the group sessions
Take medication as the main treatment instead
Diet first, then begin CBT-ED once weight drops
Avoid dieting during treatment as it can trigger binges
C.why: NG69 1.4.1 says weight loss is not a therapy target in itself, and 1.4.7 advises people having CBT-ED for binge eating disorder not to try to lose weight during treatment, because dieting is likely to trigger binge eating.

whyNot.0: Dieting during treatment is likely to trigger binge eating.
whyNot.1: NG69: do not offer medication as the sole treatment for binge eating disorder.
whyNot.2: Treatment should not wait for weight loss, which is not the target.

reteach.title: Rate every parameter, not just BMI
reteach.question: How do you decide how dangerous an eating disorder is right now?

blocks.body: MEED rates each physical sign on its own: BMI, rate of weight loss, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, postural change, SUSS, ECG and bloods. Each parameter in the red column sits in the high impending risk band and the tool directs urgent medical review, whatever the BMI. Think of a car dashboard: the fuel gauge might read a quarter, but if the oil light is on, you stop.

blocks.text: A BMI of 15 does not make a heart rate of 38 safe. Escalate on any red flag.

explain.body: Adult anorexia: CBT-ED, MANTRA or SSCM. Young people with anorexia: FT-AN. Bulimia: guided self-help (adults) or FT-BN (young people). Binge eating: guided self-help, then group CBT-ED.

test.q: Which is one of the three first-line psychological treatments for adults with anorexia nervosa in NICE NG69?
options: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR)
Dialectical behaviour therapy
Maudsley Anorexia Nervosa Treatment (MANTRA)
Binge-focused guided self-help
test.why: NG69 lists individual CBT-ED, MANTRA and SSCM for adults with anorexia nervosa.

whyNot.1: DBT is used for emotional dysregulation and self-harm, not as NG69 first-line anorexia treatment.
whyNot.3: Guided self-help is for binge eating disorder and bulimia.

explain.body: Adults: BMI under 13, loss of 1 kg or more a week, HR under 40, temperature under 35.5 C, postural HR rise over 30, QTc over 450 ms (women) or 430 ms (men), K+ under 2.5, SUSS 0 to 1.

test.q: Which result would be rated red in an adult using the MEED tool?
options: Potassium of 2.3 mmol/L
Heart rate of 52 bpm
QTc of 430 ms
Postural heart rate rise of 18
test.why: MEED rates potassium under 2.5 mmol/L as red.

whyNot.1: 50 to 60 bpm sits in the lowest risk band.
whyNot.2: A QTc of 430 ms is not above the adult red thresholds (over 450 ms in women, over 430 ms in men).
whyNot.3: A rise of 10 to 30 is amber; red is over 30.

explain.body: Use a refeeding protocol referencing MEED; train staff to spot refeeding syndrome; watch phosphate, potassium and magnesium closely in the first days. Avoid under-nutrition as well.

test.q: What does NICE NG69 require for refeeding in inpatient services?
options: Feeding held back until BMI is above 15 to limit risk
Nasogastric feeding started for every new admission
A standard refeeding procedure that avoids under-nutrition
Fasting for 48 hours before refeeding begins
test.why: NG69 1.11.10: use a standard operating procedure for refeeding that emphasises avoiding under-nutrition and refeeding syndrome, referring to MEED.

whyNot.1: Route is individual; NG69 does not mandate nasogastric feeding.

explain.body: If physical health is at serious risk, the person refuses and can only be treated safely as an inpatient, use the MHA 1983. Feeding without consent only by a competent MDT. Do not discharge solely because a healthy weight is reached.

items.label: framework if life at risk and refusing

test.q: An inpatient with anorexia nervosa has reached a healthy weight. The ward manager suggests discharge that day for that reason. What does NICE NG69 say?
options: Discharge once the healthy weight has held for 1 week
Do not discharge solely for reaching a healthy weight
Discharge at once to free the bed
Discharge when an adult's BMI passes 18.5 on two weighs
test.why: NG69 1.11.4: do not discharge people solely because they have reached a healthy weight; discharge follows the care plan and a planned move back to community care.

whyNot.0: A fixed weight period is not the NG69 test.
whyNot.2: Bed pressure is not a clinical reason in NG69.
whyNot.3: No BMI figure triggers discharge in NG69.
